newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura scandal widens with political, bank twists.
newsitem.headline: Nomura scandal widens with political, bank twists.

text.p: A payoff scandal involving Japan's Nomura Securities took a twist with possible political repercussions on Tuesday when the chief government spokesman said three cabinet ministers held accounts at the brokerage.
In another sign the scandal was widening, prosecutors raided the headquarters and homes of several officials of one of Japan's biggest banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB).
Top spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference that three cabinet members currently had "dealings" with Nomura, but said they were not getting preferential treatment.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said neither he nor members of his family living as part of his household had any business with Nomura.

Hashimoto has expressed outraged at the Nomura affair since it broke in March, not surprising since he had to resign as finance minister to take responsibility for 1991 scandals involving Nomura and scores of other brokerages.

Analysts said the political aspect, for now at least, looked like a sideshow to the main drama of the widening racketeer scandal at Japan's biggest brokerage as the nation begins its "Big Bang" financial deregulation.

Prosecutors last week arrested racketeer Ryuichi Koike and raided Nomura's head office and branches after taking in two former Nomura managing directors and another senior official suspected of violating Japan's Commercial Code and Securities and Exchange Law with payoffs to the "sokaiya" racketeer.
The investigation is focusing on whether other top Nomura executives were aware of the payoffs or whether, as the brokerage maintains, the officials involved acted on their own.

But prosecutors are also probing for signs of possible misdeeds linked to so-called "VIP accounts" set up for elite customers, including bureaucrats and politicians. Nomura has denied preferential treatment was given to the estimated 8,000 to 9,000 holders of VIP accounts.
"I have checked with the three ministers and there is no connection (to the Nomura payoff scandal)," Kajiyama said.
A DKB spokesman, meanwhile, said it would cooperate with the investigation, which Deputy Chief Prosecutor Kunihiro Matuo said was linked to the probe into the Nomura scandal.

But the bank declined to comment on media reports that it made questionable loans to Koike, who was arrested last week along with his younger brother Yoshinori Koike on suspicion of violating Japan's Commercial Code by taking some 50 million yen ($438,000) in illegal payments from Nomura.
The Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who typically extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.

On Monday, the Mainichi Shimbun reported that Koike owned about 20,000 DKB shares under various assumed names, and often attended DKB's shareholders' meeting as a "friendly sokaiya" -- one who uses his influence to stop "enemy sokaiya" from making extortion attempts at shareholders' meetings.

Japanese newspapers said DKB holds problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) linked to Koike, and that another financial firm with close ties with DKB has Koike-linked bad loans worth 1.2 billion yen ($10.5 million).
The reports said the elder Koike used the loans to buy 300,000 shares in each of Japan's top four brokerages including Nomura, and used the shares as collateral for the DKB loans.
Financial analysts said the fresh developments were embarrassing for DKB but might not hurt its business much.
For Nomura, now suffering from defections by corporate, government and individual clients, and facing probable stiff penalties and a court case, the outlook is grimmer.
Authorities have made clear they intend to mete out stiff punishment as a signal such misdeeds will not be tolerated.
